notes: Important finding: chron is discoverable enough that baseline correctly used chron spec revise and avoided hand-editing v1 without ever being taught this -- the skill's real differentiating value here is narrower than expected: the full-snapshot-not-delta convention, which only lives in format/SPEC.md and the skill, not the CLI's own --help text

The skill produces a 100% vs 66.7% mean pass rate across 3 evals, but every failure on the baseline side is a *structural* miss (no chron invocation, no frontmatter, or a delta-style spec instead of a full snapshot) -- baseline content quality/thoroughness was consistently good or even more verbose. The skill's value here is specifically the durable/machine-queryable conventions, not raw writing quality.

Eval 3's baseline result is the most interesting data point: chron's own CLI is discoverable enough that an agent with no skill guidance still found and correctly used chron spec revise, and correctly avoided hand-editing the implemented v1 file. This means the skill isn't teaching 'use revise, not a manual edit' as much as expected -- its real differentiating contribution on this eval is the full-snapshot-vs-delta content convention specifically.

Only 1 run per configuration (not the usual 3) -- stddev values here reflect variance ACROSS the 3 different evals, not repeated runs of the same eval, so they're not directly comparable to a true within-eval variance measurement. Treat this as a single-pass smoke benchmark, not a statistically robust result.

Skill adds meaningful token/time overhead (+8.2k tokens, +38s mean) in exchange for the structural pass-rate gain -- expected, since the skill instructs additional steps (vault resolution check, lint run) baseline runs skip entirely.
